agent-intent-infrastructure.title: Agent Intent Infrastructure
agent-intent-infrastructure.description: How an agent finds a service, runs a task in a sandbox, pays per request with x402, a payment carried in an HTTP request, and keeps a record of what ran.
agent-intent-infrastructure.premise: Tangle is a network where independent operators run services. These guides follow one agent call to such a service: how the agent finds it, runs a bounded task in a sandbox, pays with x402 (a payment carried in an HTTP request), and keeps evidence of what ran. A Blueprint defines the service, a Job is one call to it, and an operator runs the Job.
agent-intent-infrastructure.decision: For teams wiring external agent services into a product, each step can be designed and tested on its own; a payment receipt or a hardware attestation never proves an answer correct.
agent-intent-infrastructure.path: Start with discovery. Then come the sandbox, browser, and model router an agent works through; x402 payment and wallet prompts; the runtime record; three product comparisons; a deployed paid Job; and what hardware attestation proves.

agent-runtime-infrastructure.title: Agent Runtime Infrastructure
agent-runtime-infrastructure.description: How an agent's settings become a running worker with enforced budgets, checked output, visible progress, and a readable trace.
agent-runtime-infrastructure.premise: An agent runtime is the software that gives a model its tools, files, limits, and record of work. These posts follow one set of settings into an isolated worker, then through budgets, failures, output checks, and traces.
agent-runtime-infrastructure.decision: For teams maintaining an agent runtime: deliver settings faithfully, keep one execution path, reject budgets that cannot work, and keep the evidence when a worker fails.
agent-runtime-infrastructure.path: Start with the settings contract and one shared execution path. Then add worker visibility, isolated environments, a measured budget floor, output checks that survive failure, and a trace format another tool can read.

blueprint-agent.title: Blueprint Agent
blueprint-agent.description: Blueprint Agent is a browser coding workspace; these posts check developer quests and hackathon builds by running the code.
blueprint-agent.premise: Blueprint Agent is Tangle's browser-based coding workspace: an agent writes and runs code in an isolated sandbox. These posts judge a developer's work by what runs: a build, a test, a browser check, wallet state, or a deployed URL.
blueprint-agent.decision: For developer-relations, partner, and hackathon teams deciding whether a working artifact is better proof of learning than clicks or screenshots. Each check proves one thing; none proves a whole submission correct.
blueprint-agent.path: Start with the evidence one coding task leaves behind. Then apply it to onboarding metrics, quest design, and hackathon judging, and end with a proposed shared workbench.

blueprint-sdk.title: Blueprint SDK Guide: Run Rust Services on Tangle
blueprint-sdk.description: Package a Rust service as a Blueprint, a service definition that independent operators run, then test it, deploy it to a test network, and plan a rollback.
blueprint-sdk.premise: Tangle is a network where independent operators run services. The Blueprint SDK is a Rust toolkit for packaging, testing, and operating those services: a Blueprint is a reusable service definition, a Job is one callable unit of work, and a Service is one live configured instance run by an operator.
blueprint-sdk.decision: For Rust teams deciding whether independent operators should run their service. The guide does not prove the service's own logic is correct.
blueprint-sdk.path: The guide covers the job contract, tests on a local Tangle network, what the first testnet job must record (job identifier, output, elapsed time, artifact fingerprint), and a rollback rehearsed before production.

browser-agent.title: Browser Agent
browser-agent.description: Browser tests written as English goals that keep screenshots and page state, check the final result, and stop before a wallet signs.
browser-agent.premise: Tangle Browser Agent drives a real Chromium browser from an English goal and returns what it saw, what it did, screenshots, and the result. Each run starts from a fixture (test data prepared beforehand) and from provider state (the wallet's current account, network, and connection).
browser-agent.decision: For QA, product, and wallet teams turning English goals into release checks that stop before irreversible actions such as signing or sending a transaction.
browser-agent.path: Start with the record one run should keep. Then test a multi-page journey, turn an English goal into exact checks, test DeFi and MetaMask wallet flows, and decide when the agent should retry or stop.

building-an-ai-tax-agent.title: Building an AI Tax Agent
building-an-ai-tax-agent.description: A proposed tax preparation workflow where every number links to its source document and a person approves the return before it is filed.
building-an-ai-tax-agent.premise: These posts design a tax preparation agent that works in one isolated sandbox per client and turns source documents into linked facts, draft forms, and workpapers (the calculations behind each line). Every number links to its source, and a person approves the exact return before anything is filed.
building-an-ai-tax-agent.decision: For taxpayers, tax professionals, and software builders. The workflow is a proposed design, not tax advice, and no post describes software that files a return without a person's approval.
building-an-ai-tax-agent.path: Start with the general workflow: an index of every source document, workpapers, approval, and how to judge filing software. Then work through specific cases: crypto, foreign corporations, S corporations, founder returns, multiple K-1s, and a worked Form 5471 question.

code-auditor.title: Code Auditor
code-auditor.description: How an agent turns a scanner alert into a finding another reviewer can reproduce, with reachability and impact evidence.
code-auditor.premise: An agent takes a scanner alert, clones the repository into a Tangle sandbox (an isolated machine), and tests whether an attacker can reach the flagged code. An alert is a candidate; a finding is a claim another reviewer can reproduce.
code-auditor.decision: For security and release teams deciding whether to escalate an alert, reject it as a false positive, or keep investigating. The posts describe an evidence standard, not a live audit service.
code-auditor.path: Start with one alert worked through to a finding. Then read the report a second reviewer can rerun, proofs of concept for smart contracts, and when a scanner alone is enough.

tangle-protocol.title: Tangle Protocol
tangle-protocol.description: How Tangle coordinates operator-run services across provider selection, payment, privacy, staking, lifecycle, and result checks.
tangle-protocol.premise: Tangle coordinates services run by independent operators. A Blueprint is the service template, a Service is one configured instance, and a Job is one unit of work; the actual computation runs off-chain.
tangle-protocol.decision: For builders and buyers, this series separates provider selection, payment, privacy, staking, service lifecycle, and result checking so the protocol is not mistaken for proof of correctness.

tangle-re-introduction.title: Introduction to Tangle
tangle-re-introduction.description: A first-principles guide to Tangle: Blueprints, Services, Jobs, operators, result checks, deployment, inference, and trusted hardware.
tangle-re-introduction.premise: Tangle is a network where independent operators run services, such as model inference and code execution, coordinated by blockchain contracts. A Blueprint defines a service, a Service is one deployed instance of it, and a Job is one call to it; the computation runs on the operator's machines.
tangle-re-introduction.decision: For builders and buyers deciding whether an operator-run service fits their workload. The posts keep three claims apart: that a Job ran, that it was paid for, and that its result is correct.
tangle-re-introduction.path: Start with when independent operators are worth their cost. Then follow one request through a Blueprint, see how results are checked, build and deploy a service, add model inference and code execution, and test what trusted hardware proves.

the-instrument-problem.title: The Instrument Problem
the-instrument-problem.description: How to keep coding-agent benchmarks, behavioral signals, winner selection, and cost reports aligned with the decision they support.
the-instrument-problem.premise: An agent evaluation is a repeatable test used to compare systems or decide whether a change should ship. This series examines four ways that an otherwise precise result can answer the wrong question: an incomplete benchmark, a weak behavioral signal, a ranking rule that disagrees with release policy, and a cost total that omits workers.
the-instrument-problem.decision: For teams evaluating coding agents, the evidence helps decide what each number can support, which failures require another measurement, and whether the release decision uses the same outcome the test actually counted.
the-instrument-problem.path: Begin with the boundary of a real coding-agent benchmark. Then test a behavioral signal against chance, align the winner with the release rule, and count every model-calling role before comparing cost.

the-self-improving-stack.title: The Self-Improving Stack
the-self-improving-stack.description: How agent teams improve prompts, skills, runtimes, traces, evaluations, and models without letting weak evidence ship.
the-self-improving-stack.premise: Map the parts an agent team can change—prompts, skills, runtime, traces, evaluations, model training, and release rules—and the evidence required before promoting a candidate change.
the-self-improving-stack.decision: For teams improving agents, the series helps choose the right layer, protect fresh test cases from the search process, and keep a human release decision at the end.

when-structure-pays.title: When Structure Pays
when-structure-pays.description: Measured comparisons of one agent, repeated candidates, and supervised workers, including quality, token cost, elapsed time, and uncertainty.
when-structure-pays.premise: An agent system can spend extra computation in two ways: generate several candidates and choose among them, or add a parent process that delegates to workers. These articles compare both choices against a simpler one-agent baseline.
when-structure-pays.decision: For teams choosing an agent design, the series shows when a shared checker makes extra samples useful, when coordination adds cost without a measured gain, and what another experiment must record before the result can generalize.
when-structure-pays.path: Start with best-of-five sampling, where every candidate faces the same deterministic check. Then examine a paired supervisor-versus-solo replay that records quality, tokens, elapsed time, missing data, and uncertainty.

x402-production-runway.title: x402 Production Runway
x402-production-runway.description: Run a pay-per-request service with x402: map an HTTP payment to a Tangle Job, price and quote it, monitor operators, deploy, and recover from failures.
x402-production-runway.premise: x402 turns an HTTP 402 payment challenge into signed payment terms and a retried request. Tangle is a network where independent operators run services: a Blueprint declares the typed Jobs a service accepts, each paid request becomes one Job, a facilitator verifies and settles the payment, and an operator runs the work.
x402-production-runway.decision: For teams selling pay-per-request services: pricing, quotes, monitoring, deployment, and safe recovery when payment, facilitator, operator, or result state is uncertain.
x402-production-runway.path: Start by mapping one HTTP payment to a Job. Then choose a facilitator and set prices; quote and monitor operator work; protect private execution; and deploy, check the rollout, and judge product fit.
